catalog_quote: 2.1.3. Akzent, Intonation und Ton. Darüber sind weitere Forschungen erforderlich und augenblicklich kann ich leider nur folgendes sagen: der Akzent neigt im Dab. dazu, auf der vorletzten Silbe zu ruhen. Während meiner Untersuchung habe ich öfter den Eindruck gehabt, daß die Betonungsweise des Sts. nicht mit der des Dab. übereinstimmt, woraus sich dessen eigenartige Intonation erklären ließe. Was den Ton betrifft, liegt die Vermutung nahe, daß er phonologisch relevant ist, z.B. der Vokal des Artikels -kii/-tii wird zwar meistens lang, aber seltener auch kurz gesprochen; in diesem letzten Fall kann er nur durch den Ton von dem Possessivsuffix der ersten Person Singular unterschieden werden, vgl. dadkí 'die Leute' ~ dadkì 'meine Leute', kobtí 'der Schuh' ~ kobtì 'mein Schuh'. Außerdem wird vielleicht auch das Genus durch den Ton ausgedrückt, wie es manchmal im Sts. der Fall ist, vgl. alaŋ …

sweep_summary: Dabarre (daba1260) is not in the catalog. The only title-keyword item, Glottolog ref 635436 (Russo, Sánchez Miret & Recasens 2013b, Italian raddoppiamento sintattico), is a Glottolog mis-assignment (record itself says language code dbr was computerized from the word 'struttura') and is irrelevant (priority none). Glottolog's languoid page lists only Tosco 2012 (Somali dialect overview) and Ethnologue 2025. The primary sources were already held by the project from an earlier stage of this reading (open scans from Roma Tre's ArcAdiA repository): Lamberti 1980 'Der Dialekt von Dinsor: Af-Dabarro' (verified first-hand on the page image), Lamberti 1986 'Die Somali-Dialekte', and Gebert & Mansuur 1984. Best first-hand stress statement: Lamberti 1980 p. 8 §2.1.3 — 'der Akzent neigt im Dab. dazu, auf der vorletzten Silbe zu ruhen' (accent tends to fall on the penultimate syllable; hedged; tone likely phonemic, e.g. dadkí 'the people' vs dadkì 'my people'). Lamberti 1986 §11.1 pp. 182-183 adds a group-level mora-accent picture (Digil/May: masculines vary final vs penultimate mora, feminines final; second accent shift inconsistent). Tosco 2012 (Glottolog ref 320032) was not downloaded and is low priority for stress. Saved files and addendum under

Während meiner Untersuchung habe ich öfter den Eindruck gehabt, daß die Betonungsweise des Sts. nicht mit der des Dab. übereinstimmt, woraus sich dessen eigenartige Intonation erklären ließe. Was den Ton betrifft, liegt die Vermutung nahe, daß er phonologisch relevant ist, z.B. der Vokal des Artikels -kii/-tii wird zwar meistens lang, aber seltener auch kurz gesprochen; in diesem letzten Fall kann er nur durch den Ton von dem Possessivsuffix der ersten Person Singular unterschieden werden, vgl. dadkí 'die Leute' ~ dadkì 'meine Leute', kobtí 'der Schuh' ~ kobtì 'mein Schuh'.
new_statements.translation: Further research on this is needed and at present I can unfortunately only say the following: the accent in Dab[arre] tends to rest on the penultimate syllable. During my investigation I often had the impression that the stress placement of St[andard] S[omali] does not agree with that of Dab., which would explain the latter's peculiar intonation. As for tone, the supposition suggests itself that it is phonologically relevant, e.g. the vowel of the article -kii/-tii is mostly pronounced long but more rarely also short; in this latter case it can be distinguished from the 1sg possessive suffix only by tone, cf. dadkí 'the people' ~ dadkì 'my people', kobtí 'the shoe' ~ kobtì 'my shoe'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent tends to fall on the penultimate syllable (a tendency, explicitly provisional); in addition tone (acute vs grave on the final syllable) may be contrastive, distinguishing definite article from 1sg possessive and possibly masculine from feminine in some noun pairs, as in Standard Somali.
new_statements.exceptions: No lexical exceptions listed; author flags the statement as tentative ('neigt dazu'), notes Dabarre stress often differs from Standard Somali, and gives possible tonal minimal pairs (dadkí/dadkì, kobtí/kobtì; alaŋ 'boy'/'girl', widey, walaal 'brother'/'sister'; idə 'you'/'sheep', unnə, kar-). The typescript's 'auf die vorletzte Silbe' is hand-corrected to 'auf der vorletzten Silbe' in the scanned copy. Lamberti's later comparative treatment (1986: 182-183) frames Somali dialect accent in morae and says that in dialects other than N. Somali and Jiiddu/Garre (hence incl. Digil/Dabarre) masculine nouns vacillate between final and penultimate mora while feminines are usually final-accented, so the 1980 penult tendency should be read as a tonal-accent system not yet fully analysed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent in citation/elicited forms from two Dinsor speakers recorded in Mogadishu; tone contrasts illustrated on article vs possessive suffixed nouns; no phrase-level discussion beyond the remark on 'eigenartige Intonation'.
new_statements.identity_note: Lamberti 1980 describes the Dabarre ('Af-Dabarro') of Dinsor/Dhiinsoor town (Bay region), elicited from two Dinsor speakers in Mogadishu; this is Dabarre proper (glottocode daba1260), not the Iroole/Oroole sub-variety that Lamberti 1986 (p. 44) lists as the second subgroup of Dab. Lamberti abbreviates the variety 'Dab.' and Standard Somali 'Sts.'.

new_statements.translation: Further research is needed on this, and at the moment I can unfortunately only say the following: in Dabarre the accent tends to rest on the penultimate syllable. During my investigation I often had the impression that the way Standard Somali is stressed does not agree with that of Dabarre, which would explain the latter's peculiar intonation. As for tone, it seems likely that it is phonologically relevant, e.g. the vowel of the article -kii/-tii is usually spoken long but more rarely short; in the latter case it can be distinguished from the 1sg possessive suffix only by tone (dadkí 'the people' vs dadkì 'my people'; kobtí 'the shoe' vs kobtì 'my shoe').
new_statements.citation: Lamberti, Marcello. 1980. Der Dialekt von Dinsor: Af-Dabarro. Köln: Institut für Afrikanistik, Universität zu Köln (96 pp. typescript), section 2.1.3 'Akzent, Intonation und Ton', p. 8 (= PDF p. 10). Open scan from Roma Tre ArcAdiA repository, hdl:2307/2990.

new_statements.reading: Tentative penultimate-syllable stress (author explicitly hedges: 'tends to', more research needed), with a likely phonemic pitch/tone contrast used for grammatical distinctions (definite article vs 1sg possessive; possibly gender: alán 'boy' vs alàn 'girl', widéy 'friend (m)' vs widèy 'friend (f)'). Typescript reads 'auf die vorletzte Silbe', hand-corrected to 'auf der vorletzten Silbe' (verified on the page image). Companion comparative source Lamberti 1986 (Die Somali-Dialekte, §11.1, pp. 182-183, held by the project, scanned read) gives only a group-level historical statement: outside Northern Somali and Jiiddu/Garre, masculine nouns fluctuate between final and penultimate mora accent while feminines are generally final-accented, and in May and Digil (Dabarre's group) the second accent shift was carried through inconsistently — i.e. a mora-based pitch accent system like Somali, not a fixed-syllable stress rule. Gebert & Mansuur 1984 (Studi Somali 5, pp. 147-176, held by the project) defers phonology to Lamberti 1980. No catalog record exists for Dabarre; if entered, the classification would be 'penultimate (tentative), with lexical/grammatical pitch contrast' on Lamberti 1980 p. 8.
